title: Digital Banking and the Future of Embedded Finance: How Will AI-Powered Fraud Detection and Algorithmic Credit Scoring in Cross-Border Rails Reshape Systemic Risk?
authors: Aggarwal, L.; Saravanan, T.; Loana, A.; Alisa; Shreshta
tldr: This report examines how AI-powered fraud detection and algorithmic credit scoring in cross-border embedded finance reshape systemic risk, arguing that macro-prudential governance is needed to manage algorithmic herding and model opacity.
problem_and_motivation: The global financial system is transitioning from digitization of interfaces to a fundamental restructuring of payment rails and credit assessment architectures. AI now performs core functions in fraud prevention, credit underwriting, and payment verification, but this rapid adoption introduces structural vulnerabilities including model homogeneity, algorithmic herding, and cross-border data opacity. Existing prudential frameworks are not fully prepared to address the systemic risks created by tightly coupled, high-speed algorithmic financial systems.
approach: Conducted a qualitative synthesis of industry reports, case studies, and regulatory guidance from institutions including BIS, Bank of England, and Financial Stability Board.
Analyzed AI applications in fraud detection using Graph Neural Networks through BIS Project Aurora and its federated learning approach.
Examined algorithmic credit scoring using alternative data sources, with case studies of Tala and Nova Credit for cross-border credit portability.
Reviewed embedded finance and real-time cross-border payment infrastructure including BIS Project Nexus and its hub-and-spoke connectivity model.
Identified six systemic risk categories: algorithmic herding, data bias, opacity and explainability, cybersecurity concentration, regulatory gaps, and governance failures.
findings: Graph Neural Networks in Project Aurora identified approximately twice the number of potential money-laundering networks compared to standard rule-based methods.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This report provides a comprehensive qualitative synthesis of how AI is reshaping the global financial infrastructure through fraud detection, credit scoring, and cross-border payments. It identifies six primary systemic risk categories arising from AI integration, including algorithmic herding, model opacity, and cybersecurity concentration. The paper bridges micro-prudential improvements with macro-systemic concerns, arguing that tighter algorithmic coupling paradoxically increases fragility. It contributes policy recommendations from SUERF and regulatory frameworks for governing AI in finance.

Algorithmic herding risk arises when institutions converge on similar AI models and datasets.

topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All topic domains were systematically scanned. The paper's core coverage spans AI-driven fraud detection (8.A, 8.B), algorithmic credit scoring (5.C, 6.A), and digital banking infrastructure (4.A, 4.B), receiving high relevance. Data privacy and security (10.A, 10.B) are addressed through federated learning and PETs, receiving high and medium relevance respectively. Mobile-first design (9.A) receives low relevance as it is mentioned only contextually. Engagement dynamics (11.A) is contextual given the focus on consumer adoption. Topics on Filipino demographics (1.A-C), culturally specific practices (2.A-D), expense categorization (3.A-C), budgeting strategies (7.A-E), savings/debt (13.A-C), and synthetic data generation (14.A-C) were considered and rejected as not directly covered.

limitations: Qualitative synthesis based on literature review and case studies without original empirical data.
No original algorithmic contributions or computational experiments conducted.
Limited depth on specific AI model architectures beyond high-level descriptions.

Case studies (Nubank, Tala) represent specific markets and may not generalize globally.
